title: Beads of prayer
hookLine: counting prayers on beads grew in the middle ages; the Orthodox use knotted prayer ropes

lines: A LOOP OF BEADS IN HER FINGERS.
cards: A grandmother's hands rest in her lap, a loop of beads running through her fingers. Her lips move. Every few seconds, her thumb slides one bead along.
In another house, in another church, a monk holds a loop of black wool tied in thick knots, and his thumb moves the same way. Bead, word. Knot, word.
Neither of them is looking at their hands. The hands keep count so the heart doesn't have to.

teach.b: Counting prayers is an old Christian habit. Tradition remembers desert monks who counted their prayers with pebbles, moving one stone from one pile to another.

teach.h: BEADS FOR THE OUR FATHER, THEN THE ROSARY.
teach.b: Later, in the West, people threaded beads on a string to count the Lord's Prayer, the Our Father, again and again.

In the middle ages these strings grew into the rosary, where Catholics pray the Hail Mary in sets, each set beginning with the Our Father, while they think about scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary.

teach.h: KNOTS THAT HOLD: THE PRAYER ROPE.
teach.b: In the East, Orthodox monks use a prayer rope, a loop of knotted wool, and with each knot they say the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. They tell a story about it.
A holy monk tied knots in a cord to count his prayers, and the devil kept untying them, so the monk learned to tie each knot as a little web of crosses, and the devil couldn't undo them.
Whatever its origin, the story says something true about these ropes: each knot is made to hold. Why repeat a prayer at all?

teach.h: PRAY WITHOUT CEASING, NOT IN VAIN.
teach.b: Paul tells one church, in the King James Bible, "Pray without ceasing." Repetition is one way people have tried to obey that line. But Jesus also says, in Matthew, "use not vain repetitions."

For that reason some Protestants are cautious about counted prayers, and pray in their own words. Catholic and Orthodox teachers answer that a prayer said from the heart isn't vain, however often it's said.
Each side reads the same Gospel seriously.

how: Catholics pray the rosary on a string of beads, alone or together, and Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer on a knotted prayer rope; some Anglicans and Lutherans use prayer beads too.

Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me
the Hail Mary, said in sets on rosary beads

games.q: you're a monk counting prayers with knots in a cord. every night, the story says, the devil unties them. what do you do?
o: tie each knot as a little web of crosses that can't be undone.
switch to counting in your head.
games.why: in the story Orthodox monks tell, the monk tied each knot as a web of crosses, and the devil couldn't undo them.

practice: Rest your hands in your lap and choose one short line: the Jesus Prayer, the first line of the Our Father, a line from a Psalm, or, if you don't pray, a single word like thanks, or the name of someone you love.
Touch your thumb to one fingertip and say the line slowly, then the next fingertip, ten times across both hands. If you lose count, start again without fuss.

wordCard.voice: Jesus Prayer. The words Orthodox monks repeat on a knotted prayer rope, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, so the hands keep count and the heart can pray.

orig.note: Greek: the Orthodox prayer rope, a knotted cord for the Jesus Prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: counting love. Your own ten fingers can make a simple prayer rope. Back tomorrow.
